boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Fort Pillow record (April 12, 1864) in Forrest's Expedition into West Tennessee and Kentucky [March-April 1864]: the attack, the surrender demand, the assault and what followed it on April 12, with the burial truce and removal of wounded on the 13th. Paducah is KY010; Union City and the April skirmishes are context. Expedition-wide captures, recruiting and loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Accounts of the killing of Black soldiers and others after the fort was carried are recorded as each source's statement; no characterization is adopted. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field gives the Union garrison as detachments from three units, approx. 600 (side bound 600), and names Chalmers's 1st Division; NPS gives 295 white Tennessee troops and 262 U.S. Colored Troops under Booth against a cavalry division of about 2,500, and the live field reads 3100 (US 600; CS 2500). Leaming gives the garrison as some 550 effective men with six guns and the attackers as some 7,000 'as nearly as I could ascertain'. Forrest's April 4 letter gives the garrison as 500 or 600; after the attack he gives his force as part of Bell's and McCulloch's brigades numbering about 1,500 and the garrison as 700, about 500 Black and 200 white soldiers.
claims.rationale: Estimates of different dates by an interested survivor, the attacking commander and a summary; the NPS count of 557 is the only itemized figure and its source is not stated. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: NPS describes a Confederate-built earthwork with a Union inner redoubt on the bluff, outworks on knolls commanding the position, rugged terrain that kept the gunboat New Era from effective support, and artillery that could not be depressed to cover the approaches. Forrest describes a crescent-shaped earthwork 8 feet high with a ditch 6 feet deep and 12 wide, a surrounding ravine and slopes the fort's guns could not rake. Leaming says the high bluffs limited the gunboat and that barracks on lower ground 150 yards from the fort could not be reached by the fort's guns.
claims.rationale: Ground and works described by the attacker, a survivor and a summary; no map verification. The earthwork predates the attack but the barracks and ground were contested during it, so the phase is left unresolved.

claims.value: Leaming says that while the flag of truce was pending Forrest moved troops under cover of a ravine and underbrush into the position he had been fighting for, and that the garrison concealed Booth's death by signing his name to the replies. Forrest says steamers were approaching during the negotiations, that he believed the request for an hour was to gain time for reinforcements, and that the Union officers doubted his presence and called the demand a trick. NPS says Bradford asked for an hour and Forrest granted twenty minutes.
claims.rationale: Conflicting interested accounts of the truce; no independent message record inspected. Neither account is adopted.

claims.value: Forrest's April 4 letter gives the garrison's horses and supplies as the reason to attack; on April 15 he wrote that the capture of Bradford at Fort Pillow, with Hawkins at Union City, had broken up the Tennessee Federal regiments in the country. His demand, as Leaming remembered it, asked unconditional surrender with treatment as prisoners of war. NPS says the Confederates evacuated the fort that evening and gained little beyond a temporary disruption.
claims.rationale: Stated aims from the attacker, a survivor's recollection of the demand, and a summary.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Major General Nathan Bedford Forrest and Majors Lionel F. Booth and William F. Bradford. Leaming says Booth commanded until killed by a sharpshooter, that Bradford then assumed command, and that the officers voted unanimously not to surrender. Forrest says Chalmers commanded the two brigades, had driven the garrison into the main fort when he arrived about 10 a.m., and that Forrest then assumed command, ordered Chalmers to advance to the slopes, sent the demand, and directed Chalmers to prepare the assault; he posted three companies under his aide Anderson in the rear of the fort.
claims.rationale: Command roles from the attacker and a survivor. Responsibility for what followed the assault is recorded in the killing-after-assault claim as each source's statement; the listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit or blame.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory. Leaming says the attackers carried the works about 4 p.m.; Forrest says the works were carried without a perceptible halt and firing ceased within twenty minutes of the charge. Forrest's April 15 telegram says the Confederate flag floated over the fort and his letter that 'We still hold the fort'; his April 26 report says Chalmers withdrew from the fort before dark, and NPS that the Confederates evacuated it that evening.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. Forrest's dispatches differ on whether the fort was still held.

claims.value: The accounts conflict, and each is recorded as its source's statement. NPS says the Confederates drove the Federals down the bluff into a deadly crossfire, that only sixty-two of the U.S. Colored Troops survived, that many accused the Confederates of a massacre of the Black troops, and that the controversy continues. Leaming says the garrison threw down its arms and surrendered, that its men were then shot down without mercy and almost without regard to color until dark and through the night, that wounded were murdered the next morning and barracks holding wounded were set on fire, and that he could not estimate those killed after surrender at less than 300. Forrest's April 15 letter says many ran into the river and were shot and drowned, that 'The river was dyed with the blood of the slaughtered for 200 yards', and that he hoped these facts would show the Northern people 'that negro soldiers cannot cope with Southerners'. His April 26 report says the garrison retreated toward the river arms in hand, firing back with colors flying, and that his rear parties stopped firing when the flag was cut down; his May 16 letter speaks of 'the so-called massacre' and his June address of a victory 'made a massacre only by dastardly Yankee reporters'.
claims.rationale: The characterization of the killing is disputed between the sources and is not adopted; no source is treated as settling it. Leaming is a wounded survivor writing nine months later with reference to the Joint Committee report; Forrest is the attacking commander. The Joint Committee report, the other survivors' reports and the Confederate subordinate reports were not inspected. No count of those killed after surrender is adopted.

claims.value: The frozen casualty field reads 654 (US 574; CS 80); the live field reads 649 (US 549; CS 100). Forrest gives his loss as 20 killed and 60 wounded in each account, and the enemy's as 500 killed (April 15 telegram), upward of 500 killed (letter to Jack), 450 to 500 killed, wounded and drowned including citizens (letter to Davis), and unknown, with 228 buried that evening (April 26 report); he reports 164 Federals, 75 Black troops and about 40 Black women and children captured. Leaming says he and some 59 others were all the surviving wounded taken off on the 13th, and estimates the Confederate loss at 500 killed and wounded.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Forrest's own figures for the garrison's loss differ between his accounts and include citizens; Leaming's are estimates. No figure is adopted.

open_questions: The Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War report (House Report No. 65), Hurlbut's No. 9, Harris's No. 10, Woodruff's No. 11, the Smith and Cleary No. 13, Lamberg's No. 14, W. T. Smith's No. 15, Van Horn's No. 16 and Ferguson's No. 17 reports, Washburn's No. 24 correspondence with Lee and Forrest, S. D. Lee's No. 25, Goodwin's No. 27 and Chalmers's No. 28 reports, Anderson's and Young's statements, the naval reports, Jordan and Pryor's Chapter XVI, and maps remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family (the NPS battle page plus the frozen Arnold rows). Nathan B. Forrest's dispatches, letters and April 26 report (Official Records Series I, Volume XXXII, Part 1, No. 26) and his June 1864 address to his troops (Volume XXXIX, Part 1, addenda to No. 22) are one family of interested Confederate accounts; Jordan and Pryor's registered history is not independent of it and was not used here. The Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses; report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge. Here the second family is Mack J. Leaming's January 17, 1865 report (No. 12), by a wounded survivor of the garrison who gives the surrender correspondence from memory.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
